background.speaker: [target]
background.text: The night of April 4th, 1967, I believe that Martin Luther King, Jr. delivered probably one of the best and most powerful speeches I ever heard him deliver. I've heard many sermons, many speeches along the way. I was at the March on Washington, the youngest speaker, and out of the ten people that spoke that day, I'm the only one still around. But I think the speech at Riverside Church was his best. He literally preached. There was hundreds of ministers, religious leaders, nuns, rabbis, and just plain, everyday people. He said in effect that he was not going to push. He said, as a nation, we talk about nonviolence here in America, and then we engage in violence abroad in Vietnam. He said in effect that the bombs that were dropping in Vietnam, they would be shattered over America. He felt good. He knew he was getting over. He literally poured out his heart the depth and essence of his soul. He felt very strongly. Dr. King believed in the way of peace, the way of love. He believed in the discipline and the philosophy of nonviolence.

background.text: I'm just going to jump to the assassination you were working with, were you with Bobby Kennedy then?

ground_truth: In 1968, I was in Indianapolis, Indiana, organizing for Bobby Kennedy, and a group of us were planning a rally in a transition neighborhood, an outdoor rally, and there was some debate about whether Bobby Kennedy should come and speak. Some of us had heard that Dr. King had been shot, but we didn't know his condition. And I, for one, kept insisting that Bobby Kennedy had to come and speak to the crowd that were waiting, and he did come and speak. And it was Robert Kennedy who announced that evening, April 4, 1968, that he had some bad news. He said, in effect, that Martin Luther King, Jr. was assassinated. And a hush came over the crowd. Some people cried, and I said to myself, well, we still have Bobby. And I started crying a little and a little more, but if it had been for Martin Luther King, Jr., I don't know. I don't know what would have happened to me, growing up very, very poor in rural Alabama. Dr. King had provided a light for some of us, provided hope for some of us. He was the embodiment of our future. Bobby Kennedy suggested that a young man by the name of Earl Graves, who was on his staff, and myself, to take a flight to Atlanta and help in preparation for the funeral. I will never forget going back to Atlanta and visiting Ebenezer Baptist Church that he co-pastored with his father. And the evening before the funeral, I went to Atlanta. I went to Atlanta. I went to Atlanta. I went to Atlanta. I went to Atlanta. And Bobby Kennedy and other members of the Kennedy family wanted to go down to the church. And it was my responsibility to lead them through the education building down a flight of stairs to view the body of Dr. King. background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: How did it personally affect Bobby Kennedy when he heard the news?

ground_truth: When Bobby Kennedy heard that Dr. King had been assassinated, he was shaken. He invited us that evening to come to his room at a hotel in Annapolis. I knew that his brother, President Kennedy, admired Dr. King. They probably had some differences, but I remember the day of the march, the day of the march, when President Kennedy invited all of us, all of the speakers, down to the White House. And he stood in the door of the Oval Office greeting each one of us, saying, you did a good job. He was beaming like a proud father. He got to Dr. King. He said, you did a good job, and you had a dream. That was my last time seeing President Kennedy. So I felt that when President Kennedy was assassinated, and later Dr. King, I felt that in Bobby Kennedy, two months after Dr. King, that something died in all of us. Something died in America. Some of that sense of hope and faith died.

background.text: And afterwards, with the idea of the Poor People's March, if we go back a little bit, I'd go back to the idea, Mary Matt Edelman was telling us that it was Bobby Kennedy saying, King, you need this march, bring the poor to Washington. ground_truth: I remember very well being at one of the meetings discussing the Poor People's Campaign. At this time I was serving on the board of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. We met at Pasco's in Atlanta where Dr. King brought a group representing those that had been left out and left behind. There were low-income whites, low-income African-Americans, Latinos and Asian-Americans and Native Americans all meeting together, preparing to take the issues, the concerns, and the needs of poor people to Washington to camp out. People were ready. People were prepared to go and stay awhile. And at the same time, there was a struggle going on in Memphis. Dr. King hadn't planned to go to Memphis. But a young man by the name of Jim Lawson, who became our teacher during the preparation for the sit-ins and the Freedom Ride. Jim Lawson was one of these brilliant young Methodist ministers who had studied the philosophy and the discipline. Dr. King used to come to Nashville and speak. He had so much love and admiration for Jim Lawson. This young guy was just smart. He had studied Gundy. He had studied Thoreau and civil disobedience. He prepared us. So when Dr. King would come and salute the Nashville movement, he would say, Jim Lawson had a greater understanding. He had a greater understanding of the philosophy and discipline of nonviolence than anyone he knew.
